sections.text: Utilizing nanoinducers for precision degradation of bacterial protein to mitigate antibiotic resistance

Antibiotic resistance stands as a formidable global challenge to public health. Herein, we present a bacterial nanoinducer (bacNID) designed for targeted protein degradation in treating bacterial infections. Specifically, bacNID is engineered by grafting targeting peptides of MurD and SspB onto g old nanoparticles (GNPs). MurD plays a pivotal role in peptidoglycan production for cell wall synthesis, while SspB recruits SsrA-tagged proteins for degradation by ClpXP protease. The effectiveness of bacNIDs in targeted MurD degradation via ClpXP is demonstrated across both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial strains. Importantly, prolonged exposure to bacNIDs does not result in the acquisition of resistance in either Staphylococcus aureus ( S. aureus ) or Salmonella typhimurium ( S. typhimurium ), even after 25 successive treatment passages. This stands in stark contrast to the rapid emergence of robust resistance observed with norfloxacin, evidenced by a 243-fold reduction in antibacterial activity against S. aureus after just 15 passages, and a 7410-fold decrease in activity against S. typhimurium over 22 passages. Moreover, the antimicrobial potential of bacNIDs is evaluated in vivo using S. aureus -infected nonhealing skin and corneal wounds. In summary, this study unveils a potent nanotechnology-driven strategy for targeted bacterial protein degradation with promising implications for in vivo antimicrobial applications.

Introduction Antibiotics are critical in protecting individuals from severe bacterial infections by disrupting essential metabolic pathways or cellular structures 1 , 2 . However, bacteria inherently acquire resistance to antibiotics over time, despite meticulous prescription and administration practices 3 , 4 . Mechanisms contributing to antibiotic resistance encompass modifications in membrane permeability, genetic alterations affecting drug targets, enzymatic inactivation of antibiotics, and active expulsion of antimicrobial agents 3 , 5 . Consequently, antibiotic resistance represents a pervasive global menace, compromising the efficacy of conventional antibiotics against bacterial pathogens 6 . Addressing this formidable challenge necessitates the continual exploration and development of antibacterial agents endowed with innovative mechanisms of action to evade resistance mechanisms. Nonetheless, the pharmaceutical industry still faces many hurdles, with a failure rate of approximately 95% in antibiotic development, coupled with high research and development expenses, making this pursuit economically unsustainable 7 . One potentially revolutionary therapeutic approach involves the direct degradation of the protein of interest (POI), circumventing the occupancy-driven activity characteristic of traditional protein inhibitors 8 , 9 . This strategy diminishes reliance on high-affinity ligand binding, instead facilitating a catalytic-type mechanism for POI degradation 10 . Within eukaryotes, the 26S proteasome serves as a canonical organelle responsible for degrading ubiquitin-tagged proteins via a network of ubiquitin ligases 11 . Utilizing this process, a heterobifunctional molecule has been devised to harness the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) for POI degradation, termed proteolytic targeting chimera (PROTAC) 12 , 13 . Subsequently, various other heterobifunctional molecules have been proposed to degrade POI via lysosomes or autophagy in eukaryotic cells 14 – 16 . In bacteria, protein degradation occurs in part through the transfer of messenger RNA (tmRNA) reaction, representing a well-studied pathway of regulated proteolysis 17 . Within this pathway, the SsrA tag attaches to incompletely synthesized polypeptides, subsequently recognized and degraded by the bacterial ClpXP protease 18 . While ClpXP is proficient in degrading SsrA-tagged proteins, the presence of the SspB adapter enhances the ability of ClpXP to recognize and degrade tagged proteins 19 , 20 . Previous research has illustrated the concept of fused protein degradation through direct targeting of the ClpCP protease 21 . In this study, our objective is to achieve targeted protein degradation in bacteria utilizing the SspB adapter. UDP-N-acetylmuramoyl-L-alanine-D-glutamate ligase (MurD) is recognized as a prime target for combating antibiotic resistance in bacteria 22 . Working alongside other Mur ligases, MurD catalyzes the synthesis of peptidoglycan, the predominant structural component in bacterial cell walls, starting from UDP-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc, Fig. 1a ) 23 , 24 . Here, we develop a bacterial nanoinducer (bacNID) designed to specifically degrade MurD, effectively inhibiting the growth of both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. To achieve this goal, MurD-targeting peptides (pMurD) are modified on gold nanoparticles (GNPs), alongside the incorporation of a rapidly degradable SsrA peptide tag (tSsrA, Fig. 1b ) 25 – 27 . GNPs serve not only as peptide delivery vehicles but also possess the capability to circumvent potential antibiotic resistance mechanisms, including membrane permeability issues and active efflux of antibiotics. By emulating SspB-mediated degradation of SsrA-tagged proteins by ClpXP, bacNIDs can specifically bind MurD, with the SspB adapter actively binding tSsrA on bacNIDs to tether the complex to ClpX, thereby enhancing MurD degradation by ClpXP (Fig. 1c ). Treatment of both Gram-positive bacteria ( Staphylococcus aureus , abbreviated as S. aureus ) and Gram-negative bacteria ( Salmonella typhimurium , abbreviated as S. typhimurium ) with bacNIDs results in MurD degradation and cell wall damage. Remarkably, no resistance to bacNIDs is observed in either S. aureus or S. typhimurium after 25 continuous passages of treatment. In stark contrast, S. aureus rapidly develops robust resistance to norfloxacin, with a 243-fold reduction in antibacterial activity after just 15 continuous passages. The antibacterial activity of norfloxacin against S. typhimurium decreased 7410-fold over 22 continuous passages. Furthermore, the antibacterial activity of bacNIDs is validated in vivo using S. aureus -infected nonhealing skin wounds and corneal wound models. In summary, this study underscores the feasibility of inhibiting bacterial growth through targeted protein degradation, offering significant potential in mitigating the development of antimicrobial resistance. MurD specifically catalyzes the addition of D-glutamic acid (D-Glu) onto UDP-MurNAc-L-Ala. b ClpXP is a AAA+ protease complex that uses the energy from ATP to degrade proteins within bacteria. This protease complex consists of two main components: the hexameric AAA+ ATPase ClpX and the tetradecameric peptidase ClpP. Importantly, repeated use of bacNIDs does not lead to bacterial resistance.

Results Preparation and characterization of bacNIDs Due to the inherent limitations in membrane permeability of peptides, our initial step involved the synthesis of GNPs via reduction of HAuCl 4 with glutathione, followed by modification with pMurD (CIPSHTPRC) and tSsrA (CAANDENYALAA) to form bacNIDs (Fig. 2a ). Cysteine was introduced at the N-terminus of the peptides and subsequently modified onto the GNPs through gold-sulfur coordination (Fig. 2a ). We commenced by simulating the binding of pMurD to MurD of S. typhimurium through molecular docking. Notably, pMurD formed 8 hydrogen bonds with specific residues of MurD of S. typhimurium , including Glu-158, Ser-117, Asn-139, Asp-186, and Asp-347 (Fig. 2b ). Similarly, tSsrA formed nine hydrogen bonds with SspB of S. typhimurium at specific residues, such as Arg-47, Asn-54, Arg-58, and Arg-96 (Fig. 2c ). Despite slight structural disparities between MurD or SspB of S. aureus and S. typhimurium , pMurD or tSsrA demonstrated binding affinity towards them, as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 1 . In this study, GNPs served as a versatile nanoplatform for tethering targeting peptides, deviating from the conventional single-chain structure. The ratio and density of pMurD or tSsrA on GNPs could be finely tuned by controlling the feeding ratio. Subsequently, we evaluated the antibacterial activity of bacNIDs at various feeding ratios. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 2 , bacNIDs with a feeding ratio of 1:2:2 (GNPs: pMurD: tSsrA) exhibited the highest efficacy in inhibiting the growth of both S. aureus and S. typhimurium , thereby serving as the optimal formulation for subsequent experiments. Next, we examined the morphology of both GNPs and bacNIDs using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). As shown in Fig. 2d , the TEM image and distribution analysis revealed that GNPs exhibited spherical nanostructures with an average diameter of 1.7 ± 0.2 nm. The conjugation efficiency of the targeting peptides was assessed via high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), indicating an efficiency of 90% or 95% for pMurD or tSsrA, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 3a ). Notably, peptide modification did not induce significant alterations in the size of bacNIDs (Fig. 2e ), as further confirmed by UV-vis absorption analysis. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 3b , the absorbance peak of GNPs is similar to that of bacNIDs. While the zeta potential of GNPs was approximately −19 mV, it increased to approximately −5 mV upon bacNID formation (Supplementary Fig. 3c ). Additionally, we synthesized GNPs modified solely with pMurD or tSsrA (referred to as M-GNPs or S-GNPs, respectively) as control groups. TEM analysis revealed that M-GNPs and S-GNPs exhibited a distribution similar to that of bacNIDs, with most particles falling within the 1–2 nm range (Supplementary Fig. 3d ). The zeta potential of M-GNPs was positive, while that of S-GNPs was negative (Supplementary Fig. 3c ). To validate the membrane permeability of bacNIDs, we conducted confocal imaging after incubating S. aureus or S. typhimurium with fluorochrome-labeled tSsrA or bacNIDs. While free tSsrAs exhibited limited cellular penetration, bacNID-treated bacteria displayed robust fluorescence, indicating effective intracellular delivery facilitated by GNPs (Fig. 2f ). We also performed high-resolution TEM analyses of S. aureus and S. typhimurium treated with bacNIDs. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 4 , bacNIDs were clearly observed on the bacterial surface, within the cell wall, and inside the cytoplasmic compartment of both S. aureus and S. typhimurium . These TEM observations provide direct confirmation of intracellular delivery. In combination with the ultrasmall dimensions of bacNIDs, these results support that these nanoparticles likely enter bacteria primarily through a non-specific diffusion mechanism rather than membrane damage or receptor-mediated uptake. Specific degradation of MurD and antibacterial activity of bacNIDs Subsequent to incubating bacNIDs with S. aureus and S. typhimurium for 12 h, we examined the specific degradation of MurD. As shown in Fig. 3a , immunoblot data showed a dose-dependent degradation of MurD induced by bacNIDs in both S. aureus and S. typhimurium . In contrast, GNP, M-GNP, or S-GNP treatment did not exhibit any significant effect on MurD levels in either strain (Fig. 3b ). Moreover, immunoblot analyses showed that bacNIDs selectively reduced MurD levels without affecting other Mur ligases (MurA, MurE, MurG) in S. aureus and S. typhimurium (Supplementary Fig. 5 ). It is also worth noting that a single band was consistently observed in S. aureus , methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa ( P. aeruginosa ), while two bands were detected in Staphylococcus epidermidis ( S. epidermidis ), S. typhimurium , and Escherichia coli ( E. coli , Supplementary Fig. 6 ). These results suggest that the presence of two bands may be attributed to post-translational modifications or isoforms of MurD in certain bacterial species. Next, we examined the morphology of both GNPs and bacNIDs using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). As shown in Fig. 2d , the TEM image and distribution analysis revealed that GNPs exhibited spherical nanostructures with an average diameter of 1.7 ± 0.2 nm. The conjugation efficiency of the targeting peptides was assessed via high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), indicating an efficiency of 90% or 95% for pMurD or tSsrA, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 3a ). Notably, peptide modification did not induce significant alterations in the size of bacNIDs (Fig. 2e ), as further confirmed by UV-vis absorption analysis. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 3b , the absorbance peak of GNPs is similar to that of bacNIDs. While the zeta potential of GNPs was approximately −19 mV, it increased to approximately −5 mV upon bacNID formation (Supplementary Fig. 3c ).

Additionally, we synthesized GNPs modified solely with pMurD or tSsrA (referred to as M-GNPs or S-GNPs, respectively) as control groups. TEM analysis revealed that M-GNPs and S-GNPs exhibited a distribution similar to that of bacNIDs, with most particles falling within the 1–2 nm range (Supplementary Fig. 3d ). The zeta potential of M-GNPs was positive, while that of S-GNPs was negative (Supplementary Fig. 3c ). To validate the membrane permeability of bacNIDs, we conducted confocal imaging after incubating S. aureus or S. typhimurium with fluorochrome-labeled tSsrA or bacNIDs. While free tSsrAs exhibited limited cellular penetration, bacNID-treated bacteria displayed robust fluorescence, indicating effective intracellular delivery facilitated by GNPs (Fig. 2f ). We also performed high-resolution TEM analyses of S. aureus and S. typhimurium treated with bacNIDs. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 4 , bacNIDs were clearly observed on the bacterial surface, within the cell wall, and inside the cytoplasmic compartment of both S. aureus and S. typhimurium . These TEM observations provide direct confirmation of intracellular delivery. In combination with the ultrasmall dimensions of bacNIDs, these results support that these nanoparticles likely enter bacteria primarily through a non-specific diffusion mechanism rather than membrane damage or receptor-mediated uptake.

An essential requirement for the development of antibiotics is the ability to selectively kill or inhibit the growth of bacteria without causing harm to the host, known as selective toxicity. To confirm this, we conducted cytotoxicity examinations by incubating bacNIDs with selected NIH/3T3, human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), or RAW 264.7 cells. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 14a–c , treatment with varying concentrations of bacNIDs did not induce toxicity in any of the three different types of eukaryotic cells, affirming the excellent biocompatibility of bacNIDs. Additionally, sequence alignment revealed that the MurD protein of Bifidobacterium (a probiotic bacterium) shares only 27.86% sequence similarity with that of S. aureus . Consistent with this low level of homology, treatment of Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila ( A. muciniphila ) with bacNIDs did not result in significant antibacterial activity (Supplementary Fig. 15 ). The stability of bacNIDs was assessed by incubating them in 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), simulated body fluid, and simulated intestinal fluid for extended periods, followed by evaluation of their antibacterial activity. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 16 , bacNIDs retained robust activity against S. aureus and S. typhimurium after incubation, demonstrating favorable stability under physiologically relevant conditions.

It is worth noting that other nanoparticles (NPs) can also serve as peptide conjugation platforms. To evaluate this, we synthesized Pt and Pd NPs and modified them with pMurD and tSsrA, generating Pt-bacNIDs and Pd-bacNIDs, respectively. As shown in Supplementary Figs. 17a, 18a , peptide modification did not alter the morphology of Pt or Pd NPs, and both types maintained a negative surface potential. CFU assay revealed that Pt NPs alone did not exhibit cytotoxicity against S. aureus , with colony numbers comparable to the PBS group (Supplementary Figs. 17b , 18b ). In contrast, Pt-bacNIDs significantly inhibited bacterial proliferation, consistent with immunoblot data showing MurD degradation only in the Pt-bacNIDs group. Similar results were obtained in S. typhimurium , confirming the antibacterial activity of Pt-bacNIDs. Likewise, Pd-bacNIDs also effectively suppressed the growth of S. aureus and S. typhimurium by degrading MurD (Supplementary Figs. 17b, 18b ). Collectively, these data demonstrate the successful development of bacNIDs for the specific degradation of MurD proteins in bacteria, underscoring their potential as a promising antibacterial therapeutic agent.

Antibacterial mechanism and drug resistance evaluation After confirming the antibacterial efficacy of bacNIDs, we proceeded to investigate their antibacterial mechanism. Given the role of MurD in peptidoglycan synthesis for bacterial cell wall formation, we assessed the morphological changes in S. aureus and S. typhimurium using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). As shown in Fig. 4a , SEM images revealed the typical spherical structure of S. aureus in the PBS group, unaffected by treatment with GNPs, M-GNPs, or S-GNPs. Conversely, incubation with bacNIDs resulted in severe cell wall damage (Fig. 4a ). Rod-like structures characteristic of S. typhimurium were observed in SEM images (Fig. 4b ). Next, we utilized diabetic mice to establish typical chronic non-healing skin wounds, representing a significant clinical challenge. Wounds were created on the dorsal surface of diabetic mice using a biopsy punch and subsequently infected with S. aureus . In vivo anti-infectious efficacy of bacNIDs in S. typhimurium -induced colitis model To directly assess the antibacterial efficacy of bacNIDs against S. typhimurium in vivo, we established a mouse infection model. After successful bacterial colonization, bacNIDs were orally administered to mice twice at 12-h intervals (100 mg/kg per dose), maintaining the same daily dosage throughout the treatment period. Ciprofloxacin treatment was included as a positive control. In the untreated infection group, no mortality was observed until day 5 post-infection, and by day 10 only 50% of the animals survived (Supplementary Fig. 32a ). In contrast, all mice treated with bacNIDs or Ciprofloxacin survived throughout the 10-day observation period (Supplementary Fig. 32a ). Body weight monitoring revealed that S. typhimurium infection led to a marked reduction in body weight, whereas bacNIDs or Ciprofloxacin treatment significantly restored weight loss (Supplementary Fig. 32b ). Similarly, colon length-significantly shortened in the infection group compared with healthy PBS controls-was restored by bacNID or Ciprofloxacin treatment (Supplementary Fig. 32c, d ). Histopathological analyses further supported these protective effects. Infected mice exhibited submucosal edema, depletion of goblet cells, and severe damage to intestinal villi, whereas animals treated with bacNIDs or Ciprofloxacin displayed preserved villi architecture, normal goblet cell numbers, and only mild edema, comparable to healthy controls (Supplementary Fig. 32e ). Consistently, cytokine measurements showed significantly lower levels of IL-6 and TNF-α in colon tissue from bacNID- or Ciprofloxacin-treated mice than in the untreated infection group (Supplementary Fig. 33 ). Hematological analysis revealed no significant differences between bacNID-treated and control groups (Supplementary Fig. 34a ). Moreover, liver, kidney, and cardiac function markers remained within normal ranges, indicating that bacNIDs did not induce systemic toxicity (Supplementary Fig. 34b ). Taken together, these results demonstrate that bacNIDs provide strong protection in an S. typhimurium infection model, comparable to Ciprofloxacin, thereby validating the in vivo antibacterial efficacy of our nanoplatform.

Discussion In summary, we have developed a targeted protein degradation nanodrug, bacNID, designed to inhibit the growth of both Gram-positive ( S. aureus ) and Gram-negative ( S. typhimurium ) bacteria. BacNID induces proximity between the target protein MurD and the SspB adapter in bacteria. SspB facilitates ClpXP degradation of SsrA-tagged proteins, resulting in specific degradation of MurD by ClpXP in bacNID-treated S. aureus and S. typhimurium . This degradation disrupts the main structural polymer of the bacterial cell wall, effectively inhibiting bacterial growth. Importantly, treatment with bacNIDs did not induce resistance in S. aureus or S. typhimurium after continuous 25 passages, contrasting with the rapid development of resistance to norfloxacin observed in these bacteria. The antibacterial efficacy of bacNIDs was further validated in three in vivo animal models, demonstrating their effectiveness in inhibiting S. aureus -infected nonhealing skin wounds and corneal wounds. Overall, this study highlights the potential of targeted protein degradation as a potent strategy for combating various infections while mitigating the development of antibiotic resistance.

After staining, the bacterial suspension was centrifuged to remove the materials and dyes in the medium and washed three times with PBS. Synthesis of Pd and Pt NPs To synthesize Pt NPs, 2 mL of 50 mM chloroplatinic acid hexahydrate (H 2 PtCl 6 ·6H 2 O) was dissolved in 18 mL of ethylene glycol. Next, dissolve 57 mg of sodium tetrachloropalladate (II) (Na 2 PdCl 4 ) in 3 mL of deionized water and add it to the reaction mixture, followed by heating in an oil bath at 80 °C for 3 h. Synthesis of Pd and Pt NPs To synthesize Pt NPs, 2 mL of 50 mM chloroplatinic acid hexahydrate (H 2 PtCl 6 ·6H 2 O) was dissolved in 18 mL of ethylene glycol. This solution was mixed with 200 mg of polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) in a round-bottom flask. The mixture was heated at 180 °C in an oil bath for 10 min. After cooling, 40 mL of acetone was added to precipitate the nanoparticles. The precipitate was collected by centrifugation at 11,000 rpm for 5 min and washed with acetone and n-hexane to yield purified Pt NPs. The synthesis of Pd NPs was adapted from a previously reported method 34 . The detailed procedure is as follows: Dissolve 105 mg of polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP), 60 mg of L-ascorbic acid, and 300 mg of potassium bromide (KBr) in 8 mL of deionized water, then heat the solution in an oil bath at 80 °C for 5 min. Next, dissolve 57 mg of sodium tetrachloropalladate (II) (Na 2 PdCl 4 ) in 3 mL of deionized water and add it to the reaction mixture, followed by heating in an oil bath at 80 °C for 3 h. After the reaction is complete, add 30 mL of acetone and centrifuge the mixture at 13,000 rpm for 5 min. Discard the supernatant and wash the precipitate with ethanol and acetone.

BALB/c mice or db/db mice (female, 6 weeks old) were used for the antibacterial study. Wound was prepared on the backbone of each mouse with a surgical scalpel over the surface as a circle (diameter of 10 mm). The mice ( n = 5) were randomly divided into four groups: PBS, GNPs, M-GNPs, S-GNPs or bacNIDs group. S. aureus suspension (1 × 10 8 CFU/mL, 50 μL) was used to infect the skin wound of all mice. The changes in the size of wounds were monitored by a video camera throughout the treatment process. Wound diameter was measured by a vernier caliper every 2 days. After 7 (BALB/c mice) or 12 (db/db mice) days, the tissue samples were harvested for pathological histology and immunohistochemistry analysis.
